title: Why can't you tickle yourself?
hook: Try to tickle your own ribs. Go ahead. Nothing happens, right? Yet when a friend wiggles their fingers at you, you're laughing before they even touch you. Why can't you tickle yourself?
notes: Claims follow the research pack: Wikipedia 'Tickling' (knismesis and gargalesis, dogs, horses, primates and rats; Zotterman 1939; ticklish areas; Aristotle, Darwin, Galileo; Blakemore and colleagues 1998; Christenfeld and Harris tickle machine; self-knismesis; schizophrenia and schizotypal traits; bonding, J. C. Gregory 1924, Donald W. Black, combat-play hypotheses; survey of 84 students: 32 / 32 / 36 percent), Wikipedia 'Efference copy' (efference, forward model, Helmholtz 19th century, Sherrington 1900 and the 75 years, von Holst and Mittelstaedt 1950 and the 180 degree fly, gaze stability, grip force, electric fish, corollary discharge, robot delay experiments) and the PubMed review 'The extraordinary enigma of ordinary tickle behavior' (Socrates to Darwin, two millennia, scarce experimentation).
Hypotheses about why tickling exists are hedged; the review states the purpose is still unknown.

beats.narration: Try to tickle your own ribs. Go ahead. Nothing happens, right? Yet when a friend wiggles their fingers at you, you're laughing before they even touch you. Why can't you tickle yourself? The answer is one of your brain's cleverest tricks.
Think about how strange that is. Same fingers, same skin, even the same movement. So something inside your head must decide whether a touch is ticklish, before the hand even arrives.

In this episode, we'll meet the two kinds of tickle, an ancient puzzle that stumped great thinkers, a copy machine hidden inside your brain, a tickling robot, and finally, the big question of why tickles exist at all.

Scientists actually split tickles into two kinds. The first is called knismesis. It's the light, moving itch you feel when an insect crawls across your arm. It's mildly annoying, and it usually doesn't make you laugh.

Plenty of animals feel it too. Scratch a dog in the saddle region of its back, and its hind leg starts a rhythmic, reflexive twitch. Horses twitch a special skin muscle when insects land on their sides.

The second kind is called gargalesis. That's the deeper, firmer tickle that makes you burst out laughing. It's thought to be limited to humans and other primates, although some research suggests rats can be tickled this way too. And this is the kind you can't do to yourself.

So what carries a tickle to your brain? In 1939, Yngve Zotterman stroked cats' skin with cotton wool while recording their nerves. He found the tickling sensation depended partly on the nerves that carry pain. Tickle may also depend on the nerves for touch.

Now here's something most people never notice. The most sensitive skin is not the most ticklish. Your palm feels touch far better than your feet, yet most people find the soles of their feet the most ticklish spot. Next come the armpits, the neck, under the chin, and the ribs.

This isn't a new question. The Greek philosopher Aristotle asked it in a work called Problems. His answer? Laughter comes from being surprised, and being surprised means being fooled. And nobody can fool themselves.

Charles Darwin had a similar idea. He noticed that for a tickle to work, the person being tickled must not know exactly where the touch will land. And that, he reasoned, is why most people cannot tickle themselves. Surprise, again.

Galileo was puzzled too. A feather drawn over your skin moves the same way everywhere, he wrote, yet near the eyes, the nose or the upper lip it feels almost unbearable, while elsewhere you barely notice it. The tickle, he concluded, belongs to us, not to the feather.

Socrates, Aristotle, Bacon, Galileo, Descartes and Darwin all wondered about tickling. But after two millennia of interest, real experiments are still surprisingly rare. To finally crack the self-tickle puzzle, scientists needed to look inside the brain itself.

Here's the key idea. Every time you decide to move, your brain sends a command out to your muscles. Scientists call that outgoing signal an efference. But your brain doesn't just fire it off and forget it. It quietly keeps a copy, called an efference copy.

That copy works like a forecast. Fed into what scientists call a forward model, it lets your brain predict what your own movement is about to feel like. Then the real sensations arrive, and your brain compares them with the forecast.

The first person to propose these copies was Hermann von Helmholtz, in the middle of the 19th century. He pointed out that when you gently press on your own eyeball, the world seems to move. But when your eye muscles move your eyes, the world stays perfectly still.

Why the difference? When your eye muscles do the moving, your brain has a copy of the command, so it expects the view to shift and corrects for it. A push from your finger comes with no copy, so nothing is corrected, and the world appears to jump.

Not everyone agreed. In 1900, Charles Sherrington, a founder of modern motor science, argued that muscles sense their own movements, so no copies were needed. But here's the surprising part: his view won, and the idea of efference copies was dropped for the next 75 years.

Then, in 1950, Erich von Holst and Horst Mittelstaedt tried a bold experiment. They rotated a fly's head 180 degrees, flipping its view of the world. Now, whenever the fly moved by itself, it saw the world moving too, because the copy no longer matched what its eyes reported.

Today we know these copies are at work all over the body. They help keep your gaze steady while your head moves. They let your grip predict the load when you lift and swing something. Electric fish even use them to ignore their own electric pulses while sensing other fish.

There's even a special version called corollary discharge. It's sent into the sensory pathway at the same moment as the movement command, to cancel out the signals your own movement creates. In other words, your brain mutes the sensations it already saw coming.

Now we can finally return to tickling. In 1998, Blakemore and colleagues used brain scans to study how we tell our own touches from someone else's. Volunteers steered a tickling robot with a joystick. Even with a machine doing the touching, they could not make themselves laugh.

The idea is that your cerebellum sends the touch area of your cortex precise information about where the tickle will land, and what it should feel like. Then a mechanism scientists still don't fully understand turns the tickle feeling down.

And this is where it gets strange. Later experiments added a delay between the volunteer's movement and the robot's touch. Suddenly the touch no longer matched the brain's forecast, and people felt it as more tickly. Their own touch was treated as if it came from outside.

So that's the solution. Scientists think that when the predicted feeling matches the real feeling, the brain dials it down. When they don't match, whether because of a delay or because someone else is in control, the brain can't predict the touch, and you get the full tickle.

Is it really about surprise, or about who's tickling you? Christenfeld and Harris tested this with a mechanical tickle machine. People laughed just as much when they believed a machine was tickling them as when they thought it was a person. Harris suggests tickling is a reflex, like being startled, that depends on surprise.

You've probably seen this yourself. Very ticklish people often start laughing before anyone even touches them. Some evidence suggests ticklish laughter is a nervous reaction that can be triggered by what we expect is about to happen.
And that's not all. The light, itchy kind of tickle, knismesis, can be self-made. It may work as a non-self detector that protects you from things on your skin, so it doesn't need surprise.

There's one more clue. Some people with schizophrenia can tickle themselves. And people with no diagnosis who are high in schizotypal traits are also better at self-tickling. One suggestion is that their brains are less able to track their own actions, so their own touch may not be turned down as much.
So your brain explains why you can't tickle yourself. But why do we get ticklish in the first place? Here, scientists honestly don't know yet, but there are some fascinating ideas.

visual.title: Why do we have tickles at all?

beats.narration: One idea is bonding: tickling may be a playful way for parents and children to build trust. Another dates to 1924, when J. C. Gregory proposed that our most ticklish spots are the most vulnerable in a fight, so ticklishness may push us to protect them. A third says tickle play may help children practise defensive moves.
Supporting the second idea, psychiatrist Donald Black observed that most ticklish spots sit in the same places as our protective reflexes.

But do people actually enjoy it? In a survey of 84 college students, only 32 percent said they enjoy being tickled. Another 32 percent were neutral, and 36 percent said they don't enjoy it. Strangely, some who disliked it smiled even more while being tickled.

Let's put it all together. Your brain copies every movement command it sends. It uses that copy to forecast how your own touch will feel. When the touch matches the forecast, the feeling gets muted. And since a tickle needs surprise, your own fingers just can't deliver it.

So, why can't you tickle yourself? Because your brain always sees it coming. It's the same trick that keeps your world steady and your grip just right. Next time someone tickles you, remember: you're laughing because your brain was outsmarted. Stay curious!
